implementation_notes: Python default: the entity is a plain class deriving from DeclarativeBase whose attributes carry the mapping (Mapped[str], mapped_column("email_address")) and whose metadata produces the Table; the Session is the persistence facade - it adds, loads and expires instances - so the class itself never queries or connects. MappedAsDataclass/attrs can be layered on to keep the entity a normal typed data object. These class attributes are what replaces the classic per-class mapper code; a completely metadata-free class is the imperative variant.
code_sketch:
from sqlalchemy import String
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column("email_address", String(200))

# Session owns persistence: session.add(user); session.get(User, 1)
pitfalls: Instrumented attributes shadow plain class attributes: class-level access returns a SQL expression object, so dataclass-style defaults must go through mapped_column(default=...) and type checkers need the Mapped annotations.
Lazy loads execute on attribute access, so a 'dumb' entity can still trigger I/O from a property read; DetachedInstanceError is the classic symptom outside a session.
Commit expires instances by default, causing reloads on later access - session scope must be managed by the caller, not by the entity.

variants.name: Imperative (classical) mapping with metadata outside the class
variants.implementation_notes: Classical variant for strict persistence ignorance: the Table/Column metadata is defined separately and associated with a completely plain class through registry.map_imperatively() (the modern form of mapper()), so the entity imports nothing from SQLAlchemy and can be a dataclass, attrs class or plain object. Choose it when the domain package must not depend on the ORM - hexagonal boundaries, shared model libraries - and the extra mapping declaration is affordable.
variants.code_sketch:
from sqlalchemy import Table, Column, Integer, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import registry

mapper_registry = registry()
user_table = Table("users", mapper_registry.metadata,
                   Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),
                   Column("email_address", String(200)))

class User:                      # plain class, no ORM import
    def __init__(self, id: int, email: str) -> None: ...

mapper_registry.map_imperatively(User, user_table)
pitfalls: Imperative mappings are the lesser-used style (no out-of-the-box PEP 484 support) and must be registered before first use; an unregistered class fails lazily.
Table and class are two declarations in the mapping module; without a single owner for both they drift.
